b: Javier Hidalgo, a philosopher at the University of Richmond, has developed a classroom simulation game to teach about different ancient philosophies called “Ancient Philosophy as a Way of Life.”
Generously, Professor Hidalgo has created a website to share the game with anyone who may wish to try it out in their own courses.
Ancient Philosophy as a Way of Life is a free classroom role-playing game that introduces students to Hellenistic philosophy, plus a bit of Buddhist philosophy.

The game is set around 150 BCE at the court of Menander, a king who ruled a Hellenistic kingdom that included part of the Indian subcontinent. Four delegations of philosophers (Stoics, Epicureans, Buddhists, and Skeptics) arrive at court, each claiming to offer the best way of life. Some students play the philosophers, while others play members of the court, each of whom faces a personal dilemma and must decide which philosophical school to join. The philosophers present their views, lead the court through a brief philosophical exercise, and offer advice on the court members’ dilemmas. At the end, the court members announce their allegiances and the king awards royal patronage.

There is no predetermined winner: when I ran the game in two sections of my ethics course, different philosophical factions won. Students engaged in sustained debate about the merits of the different schools and also seemed to have fun with the game.

The game takes two class sessions, one for preparation and one for play, although a third session might be useful for larger or more talkative classes. It works for classes of 7 to 30 students and assumes no background in philosophy. The goal of the game is for students to encounter these philosophies as live options rather than merely as historical doctrines. Students have to understand a view well enough to defend it against objections, apply it to concrete problems, and experiment with its practices.

The game is inspired by Reacting to the Past games (which I love!) but is shorter than a standard Reacting game and is designed to emphasize philosophical debate in particular. The website has everything an instructor needs to run the game: a student gamebook, an instructor’s manual, faction handouts, role sheets, dilemma cards, and ballots. All materials are free to download.
Check it out. Professor Hidalgo adds, “The game is still in development and I would welcome feedback from anyone who tries it.”
